**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken aloud, it was in a voice I didn’t recognize. My mother’s lips moved, but the sound that came out was foreign—soft, then sharp, like a blade being drawn. *"Liora."* It tasted like honey and ash. I was three years old, sitting on the floor of our apartment in Tel Aviv, my fingers tracing the cracks in the linoleum. The name had been chosen for me by my father, who had never met me, who had left before I was born. He had sent the letters from Jerusalem, scribbled in his own handwriting: *"For a girl who will carry the light."* I didn’t understand then that light could also be a prison.

Now, at twenty-five, I carry it like a second skin. Liora. It means "my light" in Hebrew, but in the streets of Jerusalem, where I’ve spent the last decade, it’s become something else—a warning, a joke, a curse. The boys in the yeshiva call me *"Liora the Fire"* when they want to provoke me, their voices dripping with the kind of arrogance that comes from knowing they’ll never be touched. The teachers call me *"the trouble"* when I ask questions they don’t want answered. And my own father, when he visits from the States, always says it with a smile, as if the name is a secret between them. *"You’re just like me, Liora,"* he’ll say, patting my shoulder. *"You’ve got that stubborn light."*

I don’t know what stubborn light looks like. I only know that it burns.

---

The first time I saw blood, it was mine.

I was twelve. My period came two days early, and I didn’t know what it was. I ran to the bathroom, pressed my thighs together, and watched the red seep through the cotton of my underwear like ink bleeding into paper. My mother found me there, her face pale. *"Oh, my God,"* she whispered, and for the first time in my life, I saw her afraid. She took me to the pharmacy, bought me pads, explained in a voice that was too quiet how this was normal, how it would happen every month, how I would have to learn to live with it. But she didn’t say *why*. She didn’t say that the blood was proof of something—proof that I was growing, that I was becoming something I wasn’t supposed to be.

I was supposed to be a boy.

Not that I ever wanted to be a boy. I just wanted to be *me*. But in the yeshiva, where I was sent to study Torah, where I was supposed to be "corrected," the teachers kept telling me I was "too much." Too loud. Too curious. Too *female*. They would pin me against the wall in the hallway, their breath hot against my ear, their hands gripping my shoulders. *"You’re not like the others,"* they’d say. *"You’re not like us."* And I would nod, because what else could I do? Because if I didn’t, they would hurt me more.

I learned to shrink.

---

The first time I kissed a girl, it was in the backseat of a car, the windows fogged up from the cold. Her name was Noa, and she had dark hair and a laugh that sounded like wind chimes. She was two years older than me, and she had been my friend for years—until the night she pressed her lips to mine and I realized, with a shock, that I wanted it. I wanted *her*. I wanted the way her fingers trembled when she touched me. I wanted the way her breath hitched when I whispered her name.

I didn’t tell anyone.

Not my mother. Not my father. Not even Noa, after that night, when she pulled away and looked at me like I was something she’d found in the dark. *"You’re not like the others,"* she said, and I knew she meant it as a compliment. But it wasn’t. It was a curse.

Because in Jerusalem, a girl like me—*Liora*, the girl who carried the light—was supposed to be something else. She was supposed to be quiet. She was supposed to be obedient. She was supposed to be *normal*.

But I wasn’t.

---

The first time I was arrested, I was eighteen.

It happened during the protests. The police had come in with their batons and their tear gas, and I was standing in the crowd, my voice raised with the others, shouting *"Free Palestine!"* until a hand clamped over my mouth and I was being dragged away. The charges were minor—disturbing the peace, resisting arrest—but the way they looked at me in the station, the way they called me *"the terrorist"* in the back of the van, made me understand something: I was already a monster.

Back home, my father was waiting. He had a drink in his hand and a look on his face that was equal parts horror and pity. *"You did what?"* he asked, and I could see the disappointment in his eyes, the way he already knew I had ruined everything.

I didn’t answer.

---

Now, at twenty-five, I am a writer.

Or I am trying to be. I write in a café near the Old City, where the air smells of spices and old books. I write about the things no one else will say—the way the walls of the yeshiva felt like they were closing in on me, the way Noa’s lips tasted like salt, the way my father’s voice still carries the weight of a name I never chose. I write about the blood on my hands and the blood in my veins, about the light I carry and the darkness I can’t escape.

Sometimes, when I’m writing, I think about what it would be like to be someone else. A boy. A soldier. A woman who doesn’t have to explain herself. But then I remember the weight of the name on my tongue, the way it sits in my throat like a stone, and I know I can’t be anyone else.

I am Liora.

And I am still learning to live with the light.

---

**The End.**

*(Word count: 998)*
